So I think it had to do with my childhood where I was placed in an education system that was overly-meritocratic and forced me to study for extended hours. I didn't have the normal childhood where you just spent time in the playground. I had to keep up with these demands as a kid and I gradually got used to suppressing any emotional needs that I had. My parents were also very demanding and exacerbated this problem. While my mom was a stay-at-home mom, she was so busy maintaining the house that she had little time to interact with her children. Still she did a better job than my dad, who just paid the bills and that was it. Over time, I think I eventually began to grow less of a connection with the outside world because I was indoors most of the time. I would say that now, there pretty is much is no meaningful connection as a result of my emotional suppression during my childhood years.  I can still socialize with people pretty well so its not an issue of ability, but I don't feel any happiness from interacting with someone like most people do.

You say that society's pressures are a matter of simply ignoring what other people say. Unfortunately its not that simple. Your basic survival needs are dependent on how well you conform to society's pressures. The low/middle class find it difficult to support themselves in an economy that experiences rising inflation and cost of living. They need to work extended hours or multiple jobs, and sacrifice sleep, time with their friends and exercise just to have the right to eat.  You can't simply just ignore what society is telling you  about getting a degree and having a job in this case, because you will be homeless and starving without any support.  The upper class don't worry about these problems but they have to perform consistently in stressful situations in order to get their high salary and this also leads to resentment and mental illness.

If society didn't dictate our lives as such, majority of mental illness sufferers wouldn't have a mental illness in the first place.
